title: Online Reviews of Credence Service Providers: What Do Consumers Evaluate, Do Other Consumers Believe the Reviews, and Are Interventions Needed?
pub: Journal of Public Policy & Marketing, vol. 40, no. 1, pp. 27-44
author: Shannon Lantzy · Rebecca W. Hamilton · Yu-Jen Chen · Katherine Stewart

dom.t: Service necessity: Verifiability cannot ensure proper treatment

mo.t: Credence incentives: More information may not improve service
Expert matching: Observable work may remain unsuitable
Service necessity: Verifiability cannot ensure proper treatment

kp.k: Credence services create persistent consumer quality-assessment problems
kp.d: The abstract reports doctors' objections to consumer-review platforms: consumers lack the expertise to evaluate medical-care quality. It connects this objection to the economics of information literature, which characterizes medical services as credence services whose quality consumers cannot evaluate even after consumption. This is a medical-services framework, not a finding about AI or legal services.
qs: Yet doctors have challenged the legitimacy of these platforms on the grounds that consumers do not have the expertise required to evaluate the quality of the medical care they receive.
This challenge is supported by the economics of information literature, which has characterized doctors as a credence service, meaning that consumers cannot evaluate quality even after consumption.

kp.k: Reviews often address observable experience rather than expertise
kp.d: Analysis of real online reviews finds that many claims concern experience attributes, such as promptness, that consumers can typically evaluate, rather than credence attributes, such as knowledge. The supplied abstract gives no sample size, numerical distribution or observation period, and does not claim that consumers can evaluate technical medical quality.
qs: Data from real online reviews shows that many of the claims made in real reviews of credence service providers focus on experience attributes, such as promptness, which consumers can typically evaluate, rather than credence attributes, such as knowledge.

kp.k: Consumers believe experience claims more than credence claims
kp.d: Follow-up experiments find that consumers are more likely to believe other consumers' experience claims than their credence claims. Claims supported by data also attract greater belief. These findings concern perceived credibility, not demonstrated accuracy of reviews or improved provider selection; the abstract supplies no effect sizes or experimental sample details.
qs: Follow-up experiments show that consumers are more likely to believe experience claims (vs. credence claims) made by other consumers, claims that are supported by data, and longer reviews even if they are not more informative.

kp.k: Review length increases belief without necessarily adding information
kp.d: The follow-up experiments also find that consumers are more likely to believe longer reviews even when those reviews are not more informative. The abstract thus distinguishes a feature affecting belief from the information a review provides.
qs: Follow-up experiments show that consumers are more likely to believe experience claims (vs. credence claims) made by other consumers, claims that are supported by data, and longer reviews even if they are not more informative.

kp.k: Policy intervention is considered, not established as necessary
kp.d: The authors frame the policy question around whether reviews could mislead consumers and discuss implications for consumers and credence-service providers. The supplied abstract mentions possible interventions but identifies neither a specific recommended measure nor a conclusion that intervention is necessary.
qs: Are interventions needed to ensure that consumers are not misled by these reviews?
The authors discuss implications for consumers and credence service providers and possible policy interventions.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lantzy, Hamilton, Chen and Stewart report that online reviews of credence service providers often discuss consumer-evaluable experience attributes, and that readers' belief in reviews varies with claim type, supporting data and review length.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about consumer reviews of credence services, particularly medical care; the supplied abstract makes no claims about AI or changes to legal services. The authors report that many review claims concern experience attributes such as promptness rather than credence attributes such as knowledge. They also report that consumers are more likely to believe experience claims than credence claims, claims supported by data, and longer reviews even when length does not add information. The abstract raises the possibility of policy interventions but does not specify an intervention or conclude that one is necessary.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The reported findings draw on real online reviews and follow-up experiments.
pts.d: The authors identify real-review data as the basis for their finding about the attributes consumers discuss, and experiments as the basis for their findings about which claims readers believe. The supplied abstract gives no sample sizes, collection dates, experimental procedures, effect sizes or statistical uncertainty. It also invokes the economics of information literature as background for the characterization of medical care as a credence service; the doctors' challenge to review platforms is reported context rather than a separate empirical finding by the authors.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: These are reported findings in a 2021 publication, not future predictions; no study period or forecast horizon is supplied.
pts.d: The claims concern consumer-generated reviews of credence service providers and readers' responses in follow-up experiments. The authors qualify the review-content finding as applying to 'many' claims, not all reviews, and say consumers can 'typically' evaluate experience attributes. The belief findings are comparative rather than absolute: experience versus credence claims, data-supported claims, and longer reviews, including those that are not more informative. Greater belief is not presented as proof of greater accuracy or better technical service quality.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly implicated groups are consumers writing and reading reviews, credence service providers such as doctors, and review platforms.
pts.d: Consumers write about aspects of service they can often evaluate, while prospective consumers' belief in those reviews depends on the attributes discussed, supporting data and length. Doctors and other credence service providers are the subjects of those evaluations. Yelp and RateMDs are identified as platforms hosting such reviews. The authors frame potential consumer deception as a policy question, not as an established outcome, and the abstract does not demonstrate effects on purchasing, provider revenue or clinical outcomes.
